Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound email with nested Google redirector chain (meet.google.com/linkredirect → google.com/url → adservice.google.com) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Endpoint network/DNS to KnowBe4-tracked phishing IOCs (Cloudflare Workers + .vu/.pt/.app landing domains) · [LLM] Microsoft Entra device-code authentication flow — first-seen for user (potential device-code phishing relay) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Click on Google nested-redirector or KnowBe4 IOC followed by device-code sign-in within 60 minutes for the same user · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Inbound email with nested Google redirector chain (meet.google.com/linkredirect → google.com/url → adservice.google.com) Delivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails carrying URLs that traverse the triple-chain Google redirectors documented by KnowBe4 ThreatLabs to mask the final phishing destination. Targets the SEG-evasion signature itself rather than the final IOC, so it catches new infrastructure even when the landing-page domains rotate. Rationale: Pivots on the exact triple-chain documented in the article (meet.google.com/linkredirect → google.com/url → adservice.google.com.ph) and the specific landing hosts (workers.dev / .vu / staiwooje.app). The redirect pattern is article-specific and not covered by generic SafeLinks rules. Hornetsecurity independently reported the same Google Meet linkredirect pattern in Feb 2026. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hornetsecurity.com/en/blog/google-meet-phishing/ • https://blog.knowbe4.com/uncovering-the-sophisticated-phishing-campaign-bypassing-m365-mfa
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1027

[LLM] Endpoint network/DNS to KnowBe4-tracked phishing IOCs (Cloudflare Workers + .vu/.pt/.app landing domains) Exploitation High
Alerts on any endpoint resolving or connecting to the specific phishing infrastructure published by KnowBe4 ThreatLabs (link-form-unj9.p-sm7rw6ru.workers.dev, data-cloud-ofe8.p-8yejy42o.workers.dev, vazquezfleytas.com and the other listed look-alike domains). Hits indicate a user clicked through the Google-redirect chain and reached the fake M365 / OneDrive page. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the 10 phishing landing domains and 2 Cloudflare Workers URLs explicitly listed in the article's IOC table. Highest fidelity detection in the bundle — any hit is a confirmed click-through past the Google redirect chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hornetsecurity.com/en/blog/google-meet-phishing/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS

let IocHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (IocDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort;

[LLM] Microsoft Entra device-code authentication flow — first-seen for user (potential device-code phishing relay) Exploitation Medium
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth 2.0 device-code flow on accounts that have not used that flow in the prior 60 days. The KnowBe4 article calls out device-code phishing (fake OneDrive page → real microsoft.com/devicelogin) as the MFA-bypass payload of this campaign. Rationale: The article explicitly names device-code phishing (fake OneDrive page eliciting a Microsoft device authentication code) as the MFA-bypass payload. Anti-joining against a 60-day baseline strips ordinary Azure CLI / PowerShell users while keeping the first-time-for-this-user signal that maps to a phishing victim entering a code. Corroborated by published KQL detection patterns (Joe Stocker SigninLogs query; Jeffrey Appel Storm-2372 write-up). Cross-checked against: • https://jeffreyappel.nl/how-to-protect-against-device-code-flow-abuse-storm-2372-attacks-and-block-the-authentication-flow/ • https://x.com/ITguySoCal/status/1761184877406572834
ATT&CKT1621 T1566.002 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
let Lookback = 7d;
let Baseline = 60d;
let PriorDeviceCodeUsers = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Baseline) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
    | summarize by AccountObjectId;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti PriorDeviceCodeUsers on AccountObjectId
| extend DeviceTrust = tostring(parse_json(tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails))[0])
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, DeviceTrustType, IsCompliantUser, AuthenticationProcessingDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let Baseline = 60d;
let PriorDeviceCodeUsers = union isfuzzy=true SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Baseline) .. ago(Lookback))
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
    | summarize by UserId;
union isfuzzy=true SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=leftanti PriorDeviceCodeUsers on UserId
| extend DeviceCompliance = tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).isCompliant), DeviceManaged = tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).isManaged)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserId, IPAddress, tostring(Location), AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceCompliance, DeviceManaged, AuthenticationProcessingDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: First-Seen Entra ID Device-Code Authentication For User (Device-Code Phishing)
id: 9c83b1f7-2d44-4af7-a6c5-1f0e9a7bb88c
description: Detects successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-in via OAuth 2.0 device-code flow on a user account that has not used device-code authentication in the prior 60 days. Tracks the device-code phishing payload described by KnowBe4 ThreatLabs in the Google triple-chain phishing campaign.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-abuse-trusted-google-domains/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1621
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode
    ResultType: 0
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - DevOps engineers using Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code' on a headless or remote host
  - First-time Microsoft Teams Room or shared-device enrolment
  - PowerShell module sign-ins (Microsoft.Graph) on a server without browser
level: high
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" (@properties.authenticationProtocol:deviceCode OR @properties.authenticationProcessingDetails:*Device\ Code*) @properties.status.errorCode:0
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog
| (AuthenticationProtocol=/devicecode/i OR Details=/device\s*code/i)
| EventResult=/success/i
| groupBy([UserPrincipal, SourceIP, AppDisplayName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.app) as app from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature="UserLoggedIn" Authentication.authentication_method="deviceCode" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | join type=left user [| tstats `summariesonly` count as priorDeviceCode from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature="UserLoggedIn" Authentication.authentication_method="deviceCode" earliest=-60d@d latest=-7d@d by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where isnull(priorDeviceCode) OR priorDeviceCode=0 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.app) as app from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature="UserLoggedIn" Authentication.authentication_method="deviceCode" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | join type=left user [| tstats summariesonly=false count as priorDeviceCode from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature="UserLoggedIn" Authentication.authentication_method="deviceCode" earliest=-60d@d latest=-7d@d by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where isnull(priorDeviceCode) OR priorDeviceCode=0 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] Click on Google nested-redirector or KnowBe4 IOC followed by device-code sign-in within 60 minutes for the same user Actions on Objectives High
High-fidelity correlation: a user clicks an inbound URL containing meet.google.com/linkredirect / google.com/url / adservice.google.com (or a known landing IOC) AND completes a device-code Entra sign-in within 60 minutes. This is the end-to-end signal of the KnowBe4-tracked attack actually working — the link click that ended in token issuance. Rationale: Combines the article's two highest-signal artefacts — the Google-redirector / IOC click pattern and the device-code MFA-bypass authentication — gated by a 60-minute temporal window per the OAuth 2.0 device-code expiry (~15 min default, allowing slack for the relay). A hit is essentially proof the attack chain in the article completed against your tenant. No Sigma — multi-table temporal join. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hornetsecurity.com/en/blog/google-meet-phishing/ • https://jeffreyappel.nl/how-to-protect-against-device-code-flow-abuse-storm-2372-attacks-and-block-the-authentication-flow/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Web.Web
let WindowMin = 60m;
let Clicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where Url has_any ("meet.google.com/linkredirect","adservice.google.com.ph","adservice.google.com","google.com/url","workers.dev","vazquezfleytas","edificiocristal","velvorra","furqanmustafa","unitedtechnofzmlogies","rydezyhrsysteminc","spectrhwqumbrands","rtzcoekdrporation","reliabilityinoperations","staiwooje.app","link-form-unj9.p-sm7rw6ru.workers.dev","data-cloud-ofe8.p-8yejy42o.workers.dev")
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, ClickedUrl = Url, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=inner Clicks on $left.AccountUpn == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + WindowMin)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime)
| project ClickTime, SignInTime = Timestamp, DelaySec, AccountUpn, ClickedUrl, NetworkMessageId, ClickIP = IPAddress1, SignInIP = IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ApplicationId, UserAgent
| order by ClickTime desc
let WindowMin = 60m;
let Clicks = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RecordType in (28, 29)
    | extend Url = tostring(parse_json(tostring(Parameters))[0].Value)
    | where Url has_any ("meet.google.com/linkredirect","adservice.google.com","google.com/url","workers.dev","vazquezfleytas","edificiocristal","velvorra","furqanmustafa","unitedtechnofzmlogies","staiwooje.app")
    | project ClickTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName = tostring(UserId), ClickedUrl = Url, ClickIP = ClientIP;
union isfuzzy=true SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=inner Clicks on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + WindowMin)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ClickTime)
| project ClickTime, SignInTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec, UserPrincipalName, ClickedUrl, ClickIP, SignInIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, tostring(Location), UserAgent
| order by ClickTime desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

[LLM] LiteSpeed cPanel Plugin redisAble Privilege Escalation Exploit (CVE-2026-48172) Exploitation High
Detects HTTP requests invoking the vulnerable lsws.redisAble cPanel JSON-API function being exploited in the wild for unauthenticated root privilege escalation. Anchors on the exact URL parameter LiteSpeed and CISA recommend grepping cPanel access logs for. Rationale: Anchored on cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble -- the exact URL parameter LiteSpeed and CISA tell admins to grep /var/cpanel/logs and /usr/local/cpanel/logs/ for. The function name is non-vocabulary so FPs outside scanners and admin diagnostics are minimal. Cross-checked with LiteSpeed's own advisory and The Hacker News write-up (both confirm the parameter and vulnerable version range v2.3-v2.4.4) plus PurpleOps and Rescana for impact context. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.litespeedtech.com/2026/05/21/security-update-for-litespeed-cpanel-plugin/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/litespeed-cpanel-plugin-cve-2026-48172.html • https://purple-ops.io/blog/litespeed-cpanel-plugin-cve-2026-48172 • https://www.rescana.com/post/critical-active-exploitation-alert-cve-2026-48172-in-litespeed-cpanel-plugin-enables-root-privilege-escalation
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Defender for Endpoint on Linux does not natively parse cPanel access logs.
// Fallback: hunt for the redisAble token appearing in any process invocation
// on the cPanel host (e.g. the cpsrvd dispatcher invoking the cpanel binary
// with the JSON API function name in argv/env), plus file activity on the
// cPanel log paths the LiteSpeed advisory tells admins to grep.
let ExploitToken = "redisAble";
let CpanelLogPaths = dynamic(["/var/cpanel/logs", "/usr/local/cpanel/logs"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has ExploitToken or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ExploitToken
    | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/usr/local/cpanel"
         or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cpsrvd", "cpsrvd-ssl", "lsws", "lsphp", "litespeed")
         or FolderPath has "/usr/local/cpanel"
    | extend Signal = "process-with-redisAble"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has_any (CpanelLogPaths)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("lsws", "litespeed", "lsphp", "cpsrvd", "cpsrvd-ssl")
    | extend Signal = "cpanel-log-write"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExploitToken = "cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble";
union isfuzzy=true
(
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has ExploitToken
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIP=HostIP, ProcessName, RequestData=SyslogMessage, Source="Syslog"
),
(
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has ExploitToken or Message has ExploitToken or RequestContext has ExploitToken
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SrcIP=SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestData=RequestURL, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, Source=strcat(DeviceVendor, "/", DeviceProduct))
,
(
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriQuery has ExploitToken or csUriStem has "redisAble"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIP=cIP, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestData=strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), UserAgent=csUserAgent, Source="IIS")
| extend Cve = "CVE-2026-48172", VulnerableComponent = "LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin v2.3-v2.4.4"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Glassworm C2 IP egress (Vultr + RU-hosted payload servers) Command & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections from any endpoint to the six CrowdStrike-disclosed Glassworm C2 payload servers. These IPs front the second-stage loader and the persistent WebSocket backdoor, including the port-5000 C2 + port-10000 DHT on 217.69.11.99. Cross-checked against CrowdStrike's takedown blog and Sonatype's hijacked-npm post; both list the same Vultr + Russian-range C2 set. IP-set match is the cleanest pre/post-takedown signal an org can deploy today. [LLM] Glassworm OpenVSX/VS Code malicious extension dropped to extensions folder Delivery High
Alerts when a file is written under a VS Code or Cursor extensions directory whose path contains one of the five OpenVSX extension IDs CrowdStrike attributed to Glassworm. This catches the install-time disk artifact regardless of whether the extension was installed via the marketplace UI, CLI, or a sideloaded VSIX. Rationale: Five OpenVSX extension IDs verbatim from the article's IOC table (quartz.quartz-markdown-editor + four oorzc.* entries) anchored to the VS Code/Cursor `extensions/<publisher>.<name>-<ver>` install folder shape. Cross-checked with Koi Security and Truesec writeups which list the same five OpenVSX IDs and confirm this is the disk path on all three OSes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/glassworm-first-self-propagating-worm-using-invisible-code-hits-openvsx-marketplace • https://www.truesec.com/hub/blog/glassworm-self-propagating-vscode-extension • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/inside-crowdstrike-takedown-of-a-developer-targeting-botnet/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FolderPath has_any (".vscode\\extensions","/.vscode/extensions",".cursor\\extensions","/.cursor/extensions")
| where FolderPath has_any ("quartz.quartz-markdown-editor","oorzc.ssh-tools","oorzc.i18n-tools-plus","oorzc.mind-map","oorzc.scss-to-css-compile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".vscode\\extensions","/.vscode/extensions",".cursor\\extensions","/.cursor/extensions")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("quartz.quartz-markdown-editor","oorzc.ssh-tools","oorzc.i18n-tools-plus","oorzc.mind-map","oorzc.scss-to-css-compile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Hijacked React Native / MCP npm package install (Glassworm) Delivery High
Alerts when files are written into node_modules paths for the four npm packages CrowdStrike, Sonatype, and Aikido attributed to Glassworm: react-native-country-select, react-native-international-phone-number, @iflow-mcp/watercrawl-watercrawl-mcp, @aifabrix/miso-client. The hijacked versions ship a preinstall hook so the artefact write itself = code execution context. Rationale: Four npm package names verbatim from the article's IOC table (react-native-country-select v0.3.91, react-native-international-phone-number v0.11.8, @iflow-mcp/watercrawl-watercrawl-mcp, @aifabrix/miso-client). Cross-validated with Aikido and Sonatype IOC posts which independently confirm the same package set. Filtering parent to node/npm/yarn/pnpm gates noise from random text editors opening the folder name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/hijacked-npm-packages-deliver-malware-via-solana-linked-to-glassworm • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/malicious-react-native-npm-releases-trigger-supply-chain-exposure

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","yarn","pnpm.cmd","pnpm","npx.cmd","npx")

[LLM] Glassworm persistence + temp-stage artefact drop (~/init.json, /tmp/ijewf, /tmp/out.zip) Installation High
Alerts on creation of any of the three named Glassworm filesystem artefacts: ~/init.json (persistence sentinel — prevents re-execution within 2 days), /tmp/ijewf (temp stage), /tmp/out.zip (temp archive). Filtering to node/npm/code/cursor parents anchors the detection to the developer-supply-chain delivery vector. Rationale: All three filenames (`~/init.json`, `/tmp/ijewf`, `/tmp/out.zip`) appear verbatim in the article's IOC table; CrowdStrike's takedown writeup confirms ~/init.json as the dedupe sentinel. Parent-process anchor to node/npm/code/cursor gates the home-directory init.json check (which would otherwise hit ~10% of legit dev workstations writing unrelated init.json files). Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/inside-crowdstrike-takedown-of-a-developer-targeting-botnet/ • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers
ATT&CKT1547 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FolderPath in ("/tmp/","/tmp") and FileName in ("ijewf","out.zip"))
   or (FileName == "init.json" and (FolderPath startswith "/Users/" or FolderPath startswith "/home/" or FolderPath matches regex @"^[A-Za-z]:\\Users\\[^\\]+\\?$"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","yarn","pnpm.cmd","pnpm","code.exe","code","cursor.exe","cursor","electron.exe","electron","bash","sh","zsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where (TargetFilePath in ("/tmp/ijewf","/tmp/out.zip"))
   or (TargetFileName == "init.json" and (TargetFilePath startswith "/Users/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/home/" or TargetFilePath matches regex @"^[A-Za-z]:\\Users\\[^\\]+\\init\.json$"))
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","code","cursor","electron","bash","sh","zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Glassworm Base64 payload marker (lzcdrtfxyqiplpd) in process/script content Exploitation High
Hunt for the `lzcdrtfxyqiplpd` variable-name fingerprint — Step Security's confirmed marker used across every compromised Python repo and the React Native payload — appearing in process command lines, AMSI-captured script content, or AsepValueUpdate Run-key values. This is a single-string anchor unique to this campaign. Rationale: `lzcdrtfxyqiplpd` is the article's named Base64 payload variable; Step Security (referenced by both CrowdStrike and the article) calls it the fingerprint present in every compromised Python repo — a 15-char Latin string with zero legitimate occurrences in real corpora. Single-string match is high-fidelity hunting telemetry across script content + process arguments. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/inside-crowdstrike-takedown-of-a-developer-targeting-botnet/ • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-strikes-react-packages-phone-numbers
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027

union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents"),
  (DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where ActionType in ("PowerShellCommand","ScriptContent","AmsiScanResult")
    | where AdditionalFields has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd" or ProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields, FolderPath, Source = "DeviceEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "lzcdrtfxyqiplpd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Solana RPC endpoint contact from Node/VS Code/Cursor dev tooling Command & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound DNS/network connections from Node, VS Code, or Cursor processes to public Solana RPC providers — Glassworm reads its C2 instructions from transaction memos on a specific Solana wallet, which forces every infected host to query a Solana mainnet RPC at C2 poll time. Anchoring to dev-tooling parent processes pulls this out of normal crypto-app browser noise. Rationale: Article body explicitly states the C2 channel reads transaction memos from Solana wallet BjVeAjPrSKFiingBn4vZvghsGj9KCE8AJVtbc9S8o8SC — every infected host must poll a public Solana mainnet RPC to fetch them. CrowdStrike confirms the same Solana-blockchain dead-drop mechanic. Anchoring to node.exe/code.exe/cursor.exe parents removes the browser/wallet-extension noise that would otherwise dominate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/inside-crowdstrike-takedown-of-a-developer-targeting-botnet/ • https://www.koi.ai/blog/glassworm-first-self-propagating-worm-using-invisible-code-hits-openvsx-marketplace

   or RemoteUrl endswith ".solana.com"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

[LLM] Cryptojacking lure: ZIP download from gleeze.com / giize.com SEO+AI-poisoned utility sites Delivery High
Hunts endpoint downloads of ZIP archives sourced from the campaign's attacker-controlled domains (gleeze.com subdomains, giize.com, directdownload.icu) that impersonate GPU/system utilities like CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark and PDFgear. This is the article-specific initial-access vector surfaced via SEO and AI-chatbot recommendation poisoning, not generic drive-by. Rationale: Domains gleeze.com (and subdomains direct-download/start-download/minemine), giize.com and directdownload.icu are named in the article and confirmed in Microsoft's blog as the ZIP-delivery infrastructure (Dynu dynamic DNS). ZIP + campaign-domain referrer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] ScreenConnect masquerade: msiexec.exe installing rogue vcredist_x64.dll after autorun.dll sideload Installation High
Hunts the campaign's stage-2 install where a sideloaded autorun.dll uses msiexec.exe to install a second DLL named vcredist_x64.dll, which is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. vcredist is normally an .exe bootstrapper, never a DLL pushed through msiexec, making this combination highly specific. Rationale: vcredist_x64.dll installed via msiexec.exe is named in both the article and Microsoft's blog as the ScreenConnect packaging trick; legitimate VC++ redistributables never deploy a DLL through msiexec, so the string pair is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] ScreenConnect client beaconing to attacker C2 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the campaign's attacker-controlled ScreenConnect relay 193.42.11.108 (and associated IPs 93.115.10.35, 198.23.185.238, 2.59.132.106), through which SimpleRunPE.exe and miner payloads are delivered. This pins the C2 channel specific to this cryptojacking operation. Rationale: 193.42.11.108 is named in the article as the ScreenConnect C2; the additional IPs are pre-extracted campaign IOCs. Microsoft's blog confirms the ScreenConnect client persistently contacts 193.42.11.108. Discrete IP IOCs are alert-grade. [LLM] SimpleRunPE.exe / D3F4E2A1 implant adding Microsoft Defender exclusions via Add-MpPreference Installation Medium
Hunts the implant disabling protection by registering Defender path/process/extension exclusions, tied to the campaign by either the SimpleRunPE.exe / masqueraded vlc.exe parent or the campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (also seen as mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc and install folder). The malware re-applies these exclusions if removed. Rationale: Add-MpPreference exclusion registration is named in the article and Microsoft's blog ("re-configures Defender exclusions"); pinning to SimpleRunPE.exe parent or the D3F4E2A1 campaign ID (confirmed mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc) removes the legitimate-admin noise. [LLM] Masqueraded vlc.exe launched via scheduled task with self-deleting PowerShell dropper Installation Medium
Hunts the alternate delivery path where PowerShell fetches the payload from a remote drive, saves it locally as vlc.exe to blend in, registers a scheduled task to launch it, then deletes itself. Detection keys on a vlc.exe process whose signer/company is not VideoLAN and/or that runs from a non-standard path under a scheduled-task or PowerShell parent. Rationale: The article specifies the binary is saved as vlc.exe "to fly under the radar," launched via a scheduled task, with a self-deleting PowerShell dropper. A vlc.exe outside VideoLAN's path with a non-VideoLAN signer and schtasks/PowerShell parent is the article-specific masquerade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1053.005 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vlc.exe"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !~ "VideoLAN" or FolderPath !has @"\VideoLAN\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("schtasks.exe","svchost.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\vlc.exe"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\VideoLAN\\"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("schtasks.exe","svchost.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GPU miner execution: gminer / lolMiner / SRBMiner-MULTI dropped at runtime Actions on Objectives High
Hunts execution or on-disk drop of the three GPU-mining tools the implant fetches at runtime — gminer, lolMiner, and SRBMiner-MULTI — which is the campaign's resource-hijacking endgame on high-GPU hosts. The implant also process-hollows the miner under a trusted binary and terminates if monitoring tools (taskmgr/processhacker/procexp/systeminformer) appear. Rationale: gminer, lolMiner and SRBMiner-MULTI are explicitly named in the article and Microsoft's blog as the three supported miners; their binary names plus stratum/pool args are high-fidelity resource-hijacking indicators on GPU-equipped endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

let BadHashes = dynamic(["16562974deec80e41ef57a71a6de8c03ceb393005fb1432f8d9d82c61294ef8c", "1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5", "062bb28765fbaa11f8cc341fa16e2c7f942a122d929cb41f4a0f755b4429f246", "c7425fbe6c3a4937934215c54027d4b67202d12ab490682fae03498870d66d06", "a460d00ef93c8ce70d32e48e55781af66a53328fc2dde45519be196c265de074", "db2d33c4e6e4a5c2263b56e8303c343305a94dde1fc2968304ba260acbbd9f9f", "cf3f8160eb5a5580e0c35054847e3ac4d01e9fe74fab8bc12bf6e8a40bf696b2", "69077fcf940fc5852fb32beed15636756ebc04ac971b7ed71d36251e7ea70a20", "2ee93ccbcd49ed94c65dcf52e7dcb8f0fa0a443ca24c0e0c7f79152efba657b7", "9ff07c9fafa9c03fdf69e4abf6806aa7c938b5480e7e258f227db0719ecd6386", "7035c2abeb617e828dfda1b119b8544fa9ae15a1d263d18bc5506acaf381f496", "e021662a652ba95c8778b991056696ab3c9b0f60d5e23b1e6cf73c3847db6610"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Vulnerable iOS fleet exposed to WhatsApp 0-click chain (CVE-2025-43300 + CVE-2025-55177) Exploitation Medium
Surfaces managed iOS/iPadOS/macOS devices reporting either of the two CVEs chained in the zero-click WhatsApp account-takeover (Apple ImageIO OOB-write CVE-2025-43300 and WhatsApp linked-device sync authorization bypass CVE-2025-55177). The actual exploit artifacts live in on-device iOS unified logs (resync races, ImageIO crash entries) outside SIEM scope, so this hunts fleet exposure — the only signal expressible on available telemetry — to drive emergency patching before a device is hit. Rationale: Built directly on the two CVE IDs the article names (CVE-2025-43300, CVE-2025-55177) and the iOS<16.7.12 threshold; these are the only high-fidelity, deployable artifacts since the behavioural traces (unified-log resync events, ImageIO errors, rogue WhatsApp client) are on-device iOS forensics not shipped to any SIEM. Cross-checked against Malwarebytes, SOCRadar, The Hacker News and Lookout write-ups confirming the chain, the linked-device-sync bypass behaviour, and Apple's Aug-2025 patch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2025/09/whatsapp-fixes-vulnerability-used-in-zero-click-attacks • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2025-55177-0-click-whatsapp-exploit-spyware-apple/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/whatsapp-issues-emergency-update-for.html • https://www.lookout.com/threat-intelligence/article/cve-2025-55177-whatsapp-for-ios

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
