[LLM] Angular ng-template language-server node spawning shell / LOLBin (RCE payload) Exploitation High
Catches the post-exploitation stage of both GHSA-ccq4-xmxr-8hcq vectors: the Node.js process running the Angular Language Service (loaded via --tsdk/ngserver) spawns a command interpreter or download LOLBin, indicating the malicious tsserverlibrary.js or JSDoc command-URI payload executed. The language-server node should never legitimately spawn cmd/powershell/curl children. Rationale: Ties the child shell/LOLBin spawn to a parent node process whose command line carries the Angular language-server --tsdk/ngserver tokens — a parent that has no legitimate reason to launch interpreters, making this the cleanest signal that either exploit vector's payload ran. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/angular-extension-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cryptika.com/multiple-angular-language-service-extension-vulnerabilities-enable-rce-attacks/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1203

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--tsdk","ngserver","ng-template","Angular.ng-template")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\bash.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
// node language-server context (parent cmdline not in 4688 child row — correlate via host/time in triage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

| where Account !endswith "$"

MuddyWater Uses DLL Side-Loading in Espionage Campaign Targeting 9 Countries

The Hacker News
2026-05-26 17 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Iranian hacking group known as MuddyWater has been linked to a new campaign affecting at least nine organizations across nine countries on four continents in the first quarter of 2026. The activity targeted industrial and electronics manufacturing, education and public-sector bodies, financial services, and professional services, per the Threat Hunter Team from Symantec and Carbon Black.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — MuddyWater Uses DLL Side-Loading in Espionage Campaign Targeting 9 Countries
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll · [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SAM/SYSTEM hive theft via reg.exe save under MuddyWater node/PowerShell chain · [LLM] MuddyWater data exfiltration staging to sendit.sh file-transfer service · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll Installation High
Hunts the legitimately-signed Fortemedia audio binary fmapp.exe side-loading a malicious fmapp.dll (Operation Olalampo lineage) from a non-standard directory. The rogue DLL embeds ChromElevator and beacons to attacker IP 157.20.182.49, so a fmapp.exe running outside its Program Files install path is the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader/DLL pair (fmapp.exe→fmapp.dll) plus the non-standard-path heuristic that separates the MuddyWater drop from legitimate Fortemedia audio software; pair documented by Group-IB (Operation Olalampo) and confirmed by Symantec. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/ • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "fmapp.exe"
| where FileName =~ "fmapp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ModulePath = FolderPath, ModuleSHA256 = SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel has no native image-load table; pivot on process execution of the signed loader from a non-standard path
let legitPaths = dynamic(["C:\\Program Files","C:\\Program Files (x86)","C:\\Windows"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\fmapp.exe"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any (legitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fortemedia fmapp.exe DLL Side-Loading (MuddyWater)
id: 6f0c2a3e-2b71-4f9a-9d2e-1a7c9e8b4d51
description: Detects the signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading fmapp.dll from outside its install directory, consistent with MuddyWater Operation Olalampo side-loading.

logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\fmapp.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\fmapp.dll'
  filter:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Program Files'
      - 'C:\Windows'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @Image:(*\fmapp.exe OR *\FMAPP.exe OR *\FMAPP.EXE) @ImageLoaded:(*\fmapp.dll OR *\FMAPP.dll OR *\FMAPP.DLL) -@ImageLoaded:(C\:\\Program?Files* OR C\:\\Windows*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\fmapp\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\Program Files/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/C:\\Windows/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(process_path,"(?i)\\\\Program Files")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="fmapp.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(process_path,"(?i)\\\\Program Files")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll Installation High
Hunts deliberate abuse of the signed SentinelOne binary sentinelmemoryscanner.exe to side-load a rogue sentinelagentcore.dll — chosen by MuddyWater specifically to evade signature-based detection. The rogue DLL name and any execution outside the SentinelOne install path is the discriminator. Rationale: sentinelmemoryscanner.exe → sentinelagentcore.dll is an exact named pair from the article; the rogue DLL name plus execution outside the SentinelOne directory makes this near-zero-FP, and Symantec/GBHackers confirm the deliberate security-product binary abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005

| where FileName =~ "sentinelagentcore.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "SentinelOne" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "Sentinel Agent"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ModulePath = FolderPath, ModuleSHA256 = SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel lacks an image-load table; detect the SentinelOne loader executing from a non-SentinelOne path
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\sentinelmemoryscanner.exe"
| where not(ActingProcessName has "SentinelOne" or ActingProcessName has "Sentinel Agent")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon Exploitation High
Hunts the MuddyWater node.exe-based implant chain that drops and launches PowerShell to perform reconnaissance, screenshot capture, SAM hive theft, privilege escalation and SOCKS5 reverse-proxy tunnelling. A node.exe parent spawning powershell.exe/cmd.exe is highly atypical of benign Node.js application behaviour. Rationale: Targets the article's specific node.exe→PowerShell implant chain (the unusual JS-runtime-as-loader pivot) rather than generic PowerShell; Symantec and BleepingComputer both describe node.exe dropping PowerShell recon scripts including SAM theft and SOCKS5 tunnelling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1113

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] SAM/SYSTEM hive theft via reg.exe save under MuddyWater node/PowerShell chain Actions on Objectives High
Hunts registry-hive export of the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives via reg.exe save or PowerShell, used by the MuddyWater PowerShell scripts to harvest local credentials for lateral movement. Scoped to a node.exe/PowerShell parent lineage to keep it article-specific. Rationale: Implements the article's 'SAM hive theft' step with the canonical reg.exe save HKLM\SAM pattern (plus SYSTEM/SECURITY needed to decrypt it); machine-account exclusion and hive-name scoping keep FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "reg.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "save"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security","\\sam ","\\security ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| where CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains Command & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections to the MuddyWater C2 IP 157.20.182.49 (the address the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to) and the campaign domains timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com. Elevated confidence when the initiating process is one of the side-load loaders or node.exe. Rationale: 157.20.182.49 is the attacker IP the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to (attributed by Huntress in the article); timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com are pre-extracted campaign domains. IP/domain matches are inherently high-fidelity—validate the IP against threat-intel before broad alerting as only the article/Huntress cite it. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.001

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater data exfiltration staging to sendit.sh file-transfer service Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts upload/staging of stolen data to the public file-transfer service sendit.sh, used by MuddyWater to exfiltrate collected data. Detects DNS/web connections to sendit.sh, especially from non-browser processes such as PowerShell, node.exe or curl. Rationale: sendit.sh is the specific public file-transfer service the article names as the data-staging destination; restricting to non-browser initiators (PowerShell/node/curl) separates exfil tooling from incidental user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:

detection:
    selection_ip:

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        ParentImage|endswith:

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High

("e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc",         | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667", "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc", "b21c802775df0c0d82c8cfde299084abc624898b10258db641b820172a0ba29a", "589ecb0bb31adc6101b9e545a4e5e07ae2e97d464b0a62242a498e613a7740b6"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667", "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc", "b21c802775df0c0d82c8cfde299084abc624898b10258db641b820172a0ba29a", "589ecb0bb31adc6101b9e545a4e5e07ae2e97d464b0a62242a498e613a7740b6")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-05-26 10 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) was supposed to close a critical gap in identity security. It meant that, even if an attacker possessed the account credentials, they couldn't log in without the second factor. While that logic was sound, attackers have now figured out that they don't need to steal the second factor: they just need the user to hand it over. If your workforce authenticates with

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MFA push fatigue: repeated MFA prompt denials followed by an approval · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue MFA / security-info device registration after suspicious sign-in (Entra persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

[LLM] MFA push fatigue: repeated MFA prompt denials followed by an approval Exploitation High
Hunts the MFA prompt-bombing pattern described in the article and the 2022 Cisco breach: an attacker with valid stolen credentials triggers a burst of push/MFA challenges that the user denies or that time out, then a single approval grants access. Detects clustered MFA-failure result codes for one user followed by a success in the same short window. Rationale: Uses the article's exact mechanism (repeated push-MFA prompts to wear the user down) expressed as the Entra failure codes 500121/50074/50076/50072 clustered then a success, the same pattern Cisco Talos documented in the 2022 breach. Threshold+temporal so alerting tier; no Sigma (correlation shape). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/recent-cyber-attack/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| extend Outcome = case(ErrorCode == 0, "success", ErrorCode in (500121, 50074, 50076, 50072), "mfa_prompt_failed", "other")
| where Outcome != "other"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize DeniedOrTimedOut = countif(Outcome == "mfa_prompt_failed"), Approved = countif(Outcome == "success"), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(Application, 10) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DeniedOrTimedOut >= 5 and Approved >= 1   // >=5 denied/timed-out MFA challenges then an approval in same 10m bucket
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend Outcome = case(ResultType == "0", "success", ResultType in ("500121","50074","50076","50072"), "mfa_prompt_failed", "other")
| where Outcome != "other"
| summarize DeniedOrTimedOut = countif(Outcome == "mfa_prompt_failed"), Approved = countif(Outcome == "success"), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeniedOrTimedOut >= 5 and Approved >= 1   // 500121=MFA failed/denied, 50074/50076/50072=MFA required/prompted; >=5 then a success = fatigue
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(500121 OR 50074 OR 50076 OR 50072)

[LLM] Rogue MFA / security-info device registration after suspicious sign-in (Entra persistence) Installation Medium
Hunts the persistence step from the article and Cisco breach: once a prompt-bombed login succeeds, the attacker enrolls their own device/authenticator for MFA so they retain access. Surfaces Entra ID 'registered security info' / device-registration audit events, ideally correlated to a recently risky or fatigue sign-in for the same user. Rationale: Targets the article's named persistence action — the Cisco attacker 'enrolled their own devices for MFA to maintain persistence' (confirmed by Talos) — via Entra audit OperationNames for security-info/device registration. Kept at hunting/high-FP because legitimate enrollment is common; intended to be triaged alongside the fatigue UC for the same user. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/recent-cyber-attack/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Microsoft Entra" or Application has "Azure Active Directory"
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","security info registration")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has_any ("registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","security info registration")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIP, Target, Result, ResultReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MFA Security-Info / Device Registration in Entra ID (possible attacker persistence)
id: 7c3f1e2a-9b54-4d8e-bf1a-2e6c0d4a91f7
status: experimental
description: Detects registration of a new MFA method or device in Entra ID, the persistence step seen after MFA prompt-bombing in the 2022 Cisco breach. High base rate of legitimate enrollment; correlate with a preceding risky/fatigue sign-in.
references:

  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/recent-cyber-attack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:

  product: azure
  service: auditlogs
detection:
  selection:

      - 'User started security info registration'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Routine user enrollment of a new authenticator app or phone

source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("User registered security info" OR "Add registered devices" OR "Register device" OR "User started security info registration")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Change.src) as src, values(Change.user) as actor from datamodel=Change where (nodename=Change.All_Changes) AND 'Change.object_category'="user" AND 'Change.command' IN ("User registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","User started security info registration") by Change.object, Change.action, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Change.src) as src, values(Change.user) as actor from datamodel=Change where (nodename=Change.All_Changes) AND 'Change.object_category'="user" AND 'Change.command' IN ("User registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","User started security info registration") by Change.object, Change.action, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | sort - _time
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud 'gh-token-monitor' persistence daemon (LaunchAgent / systemd) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm C2/exfil egress (masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, getsession.org) · [LLM] Package-manager process harvesting cloud metadata / Vault (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Vault :8200) · [LLM] npm/bun process writing GitHub Actions workflow files (worm secret-exfil injection) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm C2/exfil egress (masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, getsession.org) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound DNS/network connections to the Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP) worm's confirmed exfiltration infrastructure used after a poisoned npm/PyPI package executes its install-time payload. These domains are credential dead-drops, not legitimate developer endpoints, so any resolution is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's extracted domains (api.masscan.cloud, git-tanstack.com, filev2/seed1.getsession.org) plus the corroborated zero.masscan.cloud:443/v1/telemetry exfil endpoint. StepSecurity/Wiz/OX/Splunk all confirm these as TeamPCP/Mini Shai-Hulud C2-dead-drop infra; VPC flow lacks domain names so cloudwatch is empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.ox.security/blog/lightning-python-package-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/npm-supply-chain-attack-detection-analysis.html

[LLM] Package-manager process harvesting cloud metadata / Vault (IMDS 169.254.169.254, ECS 169.254.170.2, Vault :8200) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm or python reaching the AWS/ECS instance-metadata endpoints or a local HashiCorp Vault listener — the credential-harvesting step the Mini Shai-Hulud payload performs at install time. Package managers contacting link-local metadata IPs during dependency install is anomalous. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated network targets the StepSecurity write-up lists (169.254.169.254 IMDS, 169.254.170.2 ECS/Fargate creds, 127.0.0.1:8200 Vault) scoped to JS/Python package-manager parents, which is the worm's credential-access step. Sentinel ASIM network has no process field so this is best-effort and noisier there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://snyk.io/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised/

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud 'gh-token-monitor' persistence daemon (LaunchAgent / systemd) Installation High
Hunts creation of the worm's confirmed persistence component — a gh-token-monitor daemon installed as a macOS LaunchAgent or Linux systemd unit that polls GitHub every 60 seconds with stolen tokens. The filename string is a direct, high-fidelity IOC. Rationale: Direct match on the corroborated persistence-component name 'gh-token-monitor' and its LaunchAgent/systemd install locations from the StepSecurity attribution; the literal daemon name makes this near-zero-FP. Endpoint-only, so cloudwatch is empty. [LLM] npm/bun process writing GitHub Actions workflow files (worm secret-exfil injection) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a JS package-manager process (node/npm/npx/bun/yarn/pnpm) creating or modifying files under .github/workflows — the Mini Shai-Hulud worm injects a malicious workflow that serializes repo secrets via toJSON(secrets) and posts them to api.masscan.cloud, enabling self-propagation through CI. Rationale: Targets the corroborated propagation mechanism (injected GitHub Actions workflow serializing toJSON(secrets) to api.masscan.cloud) by flagging package-manager processes writing workflow YAML — file content isn't in EDR file telemetry, so the parent-process + path combo is the pivot. Endpoint-only; cloudwatch empty.
